::: {.solutions}

This clinic is **twenty exam-standard questions**, in three parts — transformations (Part 1), function of
a function (Part 2), and a harder mixed set built to push towards a **9.0** (Part 3). There are no
warm-ups. The aim is volume and speed: meet the same handful of ideas enough times that, the moment you
see the question, **the method is already in your head** before you start writing.

Two ideas cover everything below. Learn the box, then drill the questions until each one takes seconds to
*classify*.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The recall box — know this before you look at any question

**Transformations** — start from $y=f(x)$:

| Outside the bracket (acts on $y$, as it says) | Inside the bracket (acts on $x$, opposite) |
|---|---|
| $f(x)+a$: up $a$ &nbsp;·&nbsp; $f(x)-a$: down $a$ | $f(x+a)$: **left** $a$ &nbsp;·&nbsp; $f(x-a)$: **right** $a$ |
| $a\,f(x)$: vertical stretch $\times a$ | $f(ax)$: horizontal stretch $\times\frac1a$ |
| $-f(x)$: reflect in $x$-axis | $f(-x)$: reflect in $y$-axis |
| $\lvert f(x)\rvert$: flip the below-axis part **up** | $f(\lvert x\rvert)$: mirror the $x\ge0$ part into $x<0$ (even) |

**Areas:** $\displaystyle\int a\,f(x)+b\,\mathrm dx = a\!\int f + b\times(\text{width})$; &nbsp;
$\displaystyle\int_p^q f(kx)\,\mathrm dx = \frac1k\int_{kp}^{kq} f(u)\,\mathrm du$.

**Function of a function** — for any expression built from $f(x)$:
**(1)** let $w=f(x)$; **(2)** get the range of $w$ from the graph/given bounds; **(3)** find the max and
min of the ordinary function of $w$ on that range — **turning points *and* endpoints**. For "how many
solutions", solve for $w$ first, then count how many $x$ give each $w$.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Answer form.** MCQ → one letter. Turning point → coordinates $(x,y)$. "How many" → a whole number.
:::

# Part 1 — Transformations (classify it in seconds)

## Question 1

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=2^{x}$ is reflected in the $y$-axis and then translated by $3$ in the positive
$y$-direction. What is the equation of the resulting curve?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $2^{x}+3$ &nbsp; **B** $2^{-x}+3$ &nbsp; **C** $-2^{x}+3$ &nbsp; **D** $2^{-x-3}$ &nbsp;
**E** $2^{-(x+3)}$
:::

Reflect in the $y$-axis is an **inside** change: $x\to-x$. "Positive $y$-direction" is **outside**: $+3$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — reflect then translate a known curve; build the equation
:::


Reflect in $y$-axis: $y=2^{-x}$. Then up $3$: $y=2^{-x}+3$ — **B**.

*Distractors: **A** forgot the reflection; **C** reflected in the $x$-axis ($-f$) instead of the $y$-axis;
**D/E** put the $3$ inside, turning a vertical shift into a horizontal one.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

---

## Question 2

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ has a maximum at $(4,7)$. State the coordinates of the maximum of $y=f(2x-6)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $(2,7)$ &nbsp; **B** $(5,7)$ &nbsp; **C** $(5,14)$ &nbsp; **D** $(14,7)$ &nbsp;
**E** $(-1,7)$
:::

The maximum happens when [the input to $f$ equals $4$]{.hl} — so solve $2x-6=4$. Height is untouched by
an inside change.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — locate a feature after a combined inside change
:::


$2x-6=4\Rightarrow x=5$; height stays $7$. Maximum at $(5,7)$ — **B**.

*Distractor **A** computed $2(4)-6=2$, applying the transformation *forwards* to the $x$-coordinate — the
classic error. Always solve "input $=$ old input".* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 3

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=g(x)$, where $g(x)=f(x+2)-1$, is obtained from $y=f(x)$ by a single translation. By which
vector?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ &nbsp;
**B** $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ &nbsp;
**C** $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\end{pmatrix}$ &nbsp;
**D** $\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}$
:::

Inside $+2$ → **left** $2$ (opposite); outside $-1$ → **down** $1$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — name a combined transformation as a single vector
:::


Left $2$, down $1$: vector $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ — **B**.

*Distractor **A** is the trap: reading $f(x+2)$ as "right $2$". Inside changes go the opposite way.*
$\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 4

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ has a minimum at $(-2,-5)$. The graph of $y=-f(x)+3$ has, at $x=-2$, a

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** minimum at $(-2,-2)$ &nbsp; **B** maximum at $(-2,8)$ &nbsp; **C** maximum at $(-2,2)$
&nbsp; **D** minimum at $(-2,8)$
:::

$-f(x)$ reflects in the $x$-axis, which [turns the minimum into a maximum]{.hl}; then $+3$ lifts it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — reflection swaps max and min; then a shift
:::


$-f$: $(-2,-5)\to(-2,5)$, now a **maximum**. Then $+3$: $(-2,8)$. Maximum at $(-2,8)$ — **B**.

*Reflecting in the $x$-axis renames tops and bottoms — a min becomes a max. Distractor **D** kept the
height right but the wrong name.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:4cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 5

::: {.question}
How many real solutions does $\;\lvert x^2-4x+3\rvert = 1\;$ have?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1$ &nbsp; **B** $2$ &nbsp; **C** $3$ &nbsp; **D** $4$ &nbsp; **E** $5$
:::

$\lvert f(x)\rvert=1$ splits into $f(x)=1$ and $f(x)=-1$. [The graph of $f$ has minimum $-1$]{.hl}, so
$f=-1$ is reached **just once** (a tangent), not twice.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — number of solutions of $\lvert f(x)\rvert = k$; read it off the flipped graph
:::


$f(x)=x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3)$, minimum $(2,-1)$.

- $f(x)=1:\ x^2-4x+2=0\Rightarrow x=2\pm\sqrt2$ — **2 solutions**.
- $f(x)=-1:\ x^2-4x+4=0\Rightarrow (x-2)^2=0\Rightarrow x=2$ — **1 solution** (the graph just touches).

Total **3** — **C**.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "y=|x²−4x+3| meets y=1 three times: twice on the flipped dip, and once at the peak of the dip (where f touched −1)."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
C='#1f77b4'; L='#d62728'; H='#2ca02c'
x=np.linspace(-0.5,4.5,600); f=x**2-4*x+3
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4,3.6))
ax.plot(x,np.abs(f),color=C,lw=2,label='y=|f(x)|')
ax.axhline(1,color=L,ls='--',lw=1.2,label='y=1')
for xi in (2-np.sqrt(2),2+np.sqrt(2),2): ax.plot(xi,1,'o',color=H)
ax.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y'); ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.set_ylim(-0.3,3.5)
ax.set_title('|f(x)| = 1  →  3 solutions',fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*If the min had been below $-1$, $f=-1$ would give two, making four in total. Reading the depth of the
dip is the whole question.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 6

::: {.question}
Let $f(x)=x^2-5x+6$. How many real solutions does $\;f(\lvert x\rvert)=0\;$ have?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1$ &nbsp; **B** $2$ &nbsp; **C** $3$ &nbsp; **D** $4$
:::

$f(\lvert x\rvert)=0$ needs $\lvert x\rvert$ to be a **root** of $f$. [Each positive root gives two
values of $x$]{.hl} ($\pm$).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — solutions of $f(\lvert x\rvert)=0$; every positive root gives a $\pm$ pair
:::


$f(x)=(x-2)(x-3)$, roots $2$ and $3$ — both positive. So $\lvert x\rvert=2$ or $\lvert x\rvert=3$, giving
$x=\pm2,\pm3$: **4** solutions — **D**.

*If a root were negative, it would give **no** solution (since $\lvert x\rvert\ge0$); if a root were $0$
it would give one. Here both are positive, so each doubles.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 7

::: {.question}
Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^2 f(x)\,\mathrm dx = 5$, find $\displaystyle\int_0^1 f(2x)\,\mathrm dx$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\tfrac52$ &nbsp; **B** $5$ &nbsp; **C** $10$ &nbsp; **D** $\tfrac{5}{4}$ &nbsp;
**E** $20$
:::

$f(2x)$ squashes the graph horizontally by $\tfrac12$, so [the area under it is halved]{.hl}. Formally,
substitute $u=2x$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — area under a horizontal stretch; the $\tfrac1k$ factor
:::


Let $u=2x$, $\mathrm du=2\,\mathrm dx$; as $x:0\to1$, $u:0\to2$.
$$\int_0^1 f(2x)\,\mathrm dx=\frac12\int_0^2 f(u)\,\mathrm du=\frac12(5)=\frac52 \quad\Rightarrow\ \textbf{A}.$$

*Distractor **C** ($10$) doubled instead of halved — the reciprocal trap again, now in an integral.*
$\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 8

::: {.question}
Given that $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{3} f(x)\,\mathrm dx = 8$, find
$\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{3}\bigl(3f(x)+2\bigr)\,\mathrm dx$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $24$ &nbsp; **B** $26$ &nbsp; **C** $30$ &nbsp; **D** $36$ &nbsp; **E** $10$
:::

The $3$ scales the integral; the $+2$ adds a rectangle of height $2$ over [the full width, which is
$6$]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — area under $a\,f(x)+b$; do not forget the width
:::


$$\int_{-3}^{3}\bigl(3f(x)+2\bigr)\,\mathrm dx=3\int_{-3}^{3}f+2\times(\underbrace{3-(-3)}_{6})=3(8)+12=36 \ \Rightarrow\ \textbf{D}.$$

*Distractor **B** ($26=24+2$) added $2$ once instead of over the whole width of $6$.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 2 — Function of a function (substitute $w=f(x)$)

## Question 9

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ has range $0\le f(x)\le4$. Find the difference between the maximum and minimum
values of $\;\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^3 - 12f(x)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $16$ &nbsp; **B** $23$ &nbsp; **C** $32$ &nbsp; **D** $48$ &nbsp; **E** $64$
:::

Let $w=f(x)\in[0,4]$; study $g(w)=w^3-12w$. [Find the turning point, then check both ends.]{.hl}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(your mock Q18, retuned)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}

::: {.topic}
Topic — cubic in $w$ on a closed interval; turning point **and** endpoints
:::


$g'(w)=3w^2-12=0\Rightarrow w=2$ (in range). $g(2)=8-24=-16$ — **minimum**.
Ends: $g(0)=0$, $g(4)=64-48=16$ — **maximum** $16$.
Difference $16-(-16)=32$ — **C**.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "g(w)=w³−12w on [0,4]: min −16 at the interior turning point w=2, max 16 at the right endpoint w=4."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
C='#1f77b4'; MIN='#d62728'; MAX='#2ca02c'
w=np.linspace(0,4,400); g=w**3-12*w
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,3.6))
ax.plot(w,g,color=C,lw=2)
ax.plot(2,-16,'o',color=MIN); ax.annotate('(2, −16) min',(2,-16),(2.1,-14),color=MIN,fontsize=9)
ax.plot(4,16,'o',color=MAX); ax.annotate('(4, 16) max',(4,16),(2.4,12),color=MAX,fontsize=9)
ax.plot(0,0,'o',color='0.5'); ax.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('w'); ax.set_ylabel('g(w)'); ax.set_xlim(0,4.1)
ax.set_title(r'$g(w)=w^3-12w$ on $[0,4]$',fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*Distractor **A** ($16$) reported the max only, or took the min at $w=0$. The turning point gives the min;
the far endpoint gives the max.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 10

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ has range $-1\le f(x)\le3$. Find the difference between the maximum and minimum
values of $\;\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^2 + 1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1$ &nbsp; **B** $8$ &nbsp; **C** $9$ &nbsp; **D** $10$ &nbsp; **E** $16$
:::

$w=f(x)\in[-1,3]$, $g(w)=w^2+1$. The min of $w^2$ is at $w=0$ (**in range**); the max is at the
[endpoint farthest from $0$]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — quadratic in $w$ where the range includes negatives
:::


$g(0)=1$ (minimum, since $w=0$ is in $[-1,3]$). Farthest endpoint is $w=3$: $g(3)=10$ (maximum;
$g(-1)=2$ is smaller). Difference $10-1=9$ — **C**.

*The trap is to plug in only the endpoints and miss that $w=0$ sits inside the range and gives the true
minimum.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 11

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ is a single symmetric "bump" with maximum value $5$ (at $x=0$), positive
everywhere, tending to $0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$. How many solutions does
$\;\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^2 - 7f(x) + 10 = 0\;$ have?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1$ &nbsp; **B** $2$ &nbsp; **C** $3$ &nbsp; **D** $4$
:::

Solve for $w=f(x)$ first, then ask [how many $x$ give each value of $w$]{.hl}. The peak value is reached
only once.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — count solutions: solve for $w$, then count the $x$ behind each $w$
:::


$w^2-7w+10=(w-2)(w-5)=0\Rightarrow w=2$ or $w=5$.

- $f(x)=5$: only the peak — **1** solution.
- $f(x)=2$: since $0<2<5$, the line cuts the bump **twice**.

Total $1+2=3$ — **C**.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "f(x)=5 meets the bump once (the peak); f(x)=2 meets it twice. 1+2 = 3 solutions."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
C='#1f77b4'; L5='#d62728'; L2='#2ca02c'
x=np.linspace(-3,3,600); f=5*np.exp(-x**2)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4,3.6))
ax.plot(x,f,color=C,lw=2,label='y=f(x)')
ax.axhline(5,color=L5,ls='--',lw=1.2,label='f=5 (1)')
ax.axhline(2,color=L2,ls='--',lw=1.2,label='f=2 (2)')
ax.plot(0,5,'o',color=L5)
for xi in (-np.sqrt(np.log(2.5)),np.sqrt(np.log(2.5))): ax.plot(xi,2,'o',color=L2)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y'); ax.legend(fontsize=8,loc='lower center'); ax.set_ylim(-0.3,5.6)
ax.set_title('Solve for w, then count preimages',fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*A peak value always has one preimage; a value strictly between $0$ and the peak has two. That is what
makes the total odd.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 12

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ has range $0\le f(x)\le4$. Find the maximum and minimum values of
$$5-\bigl(f(x)-1\bigr)^2.$$

*Answer form: state the maximum and the minimum.*
:::

$w=f(x)\in[0,4]$; $h(w)=5-(w-1)^2$ is a **downward** parabola with vertex at $w=1$. [The max is at the
vertex; the min is at the farther endpoint.]{.hl}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — completed square in $w$; a downward parabola on an interval
:::


Vertex $w=1$ is in $[0,4]$, so the **maximum** is $h(1)=5$.
Endpoints: $h(0)=5-1=4$, $h(4)=5-9=-4$. The **minimum** is $-4$ (at $w=4$, the endpoint farther from the
vertex).

So maximum $5$, minimum $-4$.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "h(w)=5−(w−1)² on [0,4]: max 5 at the vertex w=1, min −4 at the endpoint w=4."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
C='#1f77b4'; MAX='#2ca02c'; MIN='#d62728'
w=np.linspace(0,4,400); h=5-(w-1)**2
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,3.6))
ax.plot(w,h,color=C,lw=2)
ax.plot(1,5,'o',color=MAX); ax.annotate('(1, 5) max',(1,5),(1.2,4.2),color=MAX,fontsize=9)
ax.plot(4,-4,'o',color=MIN); ax.annotate('(4, −4) min',(4,-4),(2.2,-3),color=MIN,fontsize=9)
ax.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('w'); ax.set_ylabel('h(w)'); ax.set_xlim(0,4.1)
ax.set_title(r'$h(w)=5-(w-1)^2$ on $[0,4]$',fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*A negative coefficient flips the logic of Q10: now the **vertex** is the max, and the min hides at an
endpoint. Same recipe, opposite parabola.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 3 — Push to 9.0 (harder mixed)

These are the ones that separate a 7 from a 9: an extra substitution, a hidden tangent, an endpoint that
is also a stationary point. Same two ideas — just less forgiving.

## Question 13

::: {.question}
The curve $y=2x^2-12x+23$ can be obtained from $y=x^2$ by a vertical stretch and a translation. State the
stretch factor and the translation vector.

*Answer form: a factor and a vector.*
:::

Complete the square, [keeping the leading $2$ outside as a factor]{.hl}: the number multiplying the
bracket is the stretch, the completed square gives the translation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — completing the square as a *sequence* of transformations of $y=x^2$
:::


$$2x^2-12x+23=2\bigl(x^2-6x\bigr)+23=2\bigl((x-3)^2-9\bigr)+23=2(x-3)^2+5.$$

So: **vertical stretch factor $2$**, then **translation by $\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}$** (right
$3$, up $5$).

*Watch the $-9$: it is inside the bracket, so it gets multiplied by $2$ before it leaves — that is why
the vertical shift is $+5$, not $+14$.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 14

::: {.question}
The function $f$ has exactly three roots, at $x=-3$, $x=0$ and $x=2$. How many roots does $f(\lvert
x\rvert)$ have?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $2$ &nbsp; **B** $3$ &nbsp; **C** $4$ &nbsp; **D** $5$ &nbsp; **E** $6$
:::

Only the **non-negative** roots survive, and [a root at $0$ gives one value of $x$, not a pair]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — roots of $f(\lvert x\rvert)$ when one root is zero
:::


$f(\lvert x\rvert)=0$ needs $\lvert x\rvert\in\{-3,0,2\}$. Since $\lvert x\rvert\ge0$:

- $\lvert x\rvert=-3$: impossible — **0**.
- $\lvert x\rvert=0$: $x=0$ only — **1**.
- $\lvert x\rvert=2$: $x=\pm2$ — **2**.

Total $0+1+2=3$ — **B**.

*The trap is to double everything and say $6$, or to double the zero. A negative root contributes
nothing; a zero root contributes one.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 15

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ has range $-2\le f(x)\le2$. Find the **minimum** value of
$$\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^4 - 8\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^2.$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-16$ &nbsp; **B** $-8$ &nbsp; **C** $0$ &nbsp; **D** $-12$ &nbsp; **E** $16$
:::

Let $w=f(x)\in[-2,2]$. The expression is even in $w$, so [substitute again, $t=w^2$]{.hl}, and note
$t$ ranges over $[0,4]$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a second substitution: let $t=w^2$ to handle even powers of $f$
:::


Let $w=f(x)\in[-2,2]$, then $t=w^2\in[0,4]$. The expression is
$$g=t^2-8t=(t-4)^2-16.$$
On $[0,4]$ this is decreasing to its vertex at $t=4$, so the **minimum** is $g(4)=-16$ (reached when
$w^2=4$, i.e. $f(x)=\pm2$). Answer **A**.

*The double substitution is the trick: $w\in[-2,2]$ **includes negatives**, but $t=w^2$ turns it into a
clean interval $[0,4]$ with no sign worries.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 16

::: {.question}
Given that $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3} f(x)\,\mathrm dx = 7$, find
$\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{-1} f(-x)\,\mathrm dx.$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-7$ &nbsp; **B** $7$ &nbsp; **C** $14$ &nbsp; **D** $\tfrac72$ &nbsp; **E** $0$
:::

$f(-x)$ reflects the graph in the $y$-axis; over the **matching reflected interval** [the area is
identical]{.hl}. Confirm with $u=-x$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a reflection leaves the area unchanged (over the reflected limits)
:::


Let $u=-x$, $\mathrm du=-\mathrm dx$; as $x:-3\to-1$, $u:3\to1$.
$$\int_{-3}^{-1} f(-x)\,\mathrm dx=\int_{3}^{1} f(u)\,(-\mathrm du)=\int_{1}^{3} f(u)\,\mathrm du=7 \ \Rightarrow\ \textbf{B}.$$

*The reflected limits $[-3,-1]$ are the mirror image of $[1,3]$, so the reflected graph encloses exactly
the same area. Sign care on $\mathrm du$ flips the limits back.* $\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 17

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis exactly at $x=2$ and $x=6$. State the roots of $y=f(2x-4)$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $x=3,5$ &nbsp; **B** $x=0,4$ &nbsp; **C** $x=8,16$ &nbsp; **D** $x=-1,1$ &nbsp;
**E** $x=1,7$
:::

A root occurs where [the input to $f$ is a root of $f$]{.hl}: solve $2x-4=2$ and $2x-4=6$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — roots after a combined inside transformation
:::


$2x-4=2\Rightarrow x=3$; &nbsp; $2x-4=6\Rightarrow x=5$. Roots at $x=3,5$ — **A**.

*Same principle as feature-finding: set the inside equal to each old root and solve for $x$. Do not apply
the map forwards to $2$ and $6$.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 18

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ is a single symmetric bump with maximum value $5$ (at $x=0$), positive everywhere,
tending to $0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$. How many solutions does $\;\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^2 = 4f(x)\;$ have?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1$ &nbsp; **B** $2$ &nbsp; **C** $3$ &nbsp; **D** $4$
:::

Rearrange to $f(f-4)=0$, then check whether each value is [actually attained by the bump]{.hl}.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — count solutions where one $w$-value is unreachable
:::


$\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^2-4f(x)=0\Rightarrow f(x)\bigl(f(x)-4\bigr)=0$, so $f(x)=0$ or $f(x)=4$.

- $f(x)=0$: the bump is **strictly positive** and only *approaches* $0$ — **never reached**, so $0$
  solutions.
- $f(x)=4$: since $0<4<5$, the line cuts the bump **twice**.

Total **2** — **B**.

*Do not cancel $f(x)$ from both sides — that would lose the $f=0$ case (and here throw away the very
subtlety being tested). Bring everything to one side and factor.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 19

::: {.question}
Let $f(x)=x^2-2x-3$, which has minimum value $-4$. How many real solutions does
$\;\lvert f(x)\rvert = 4\;$ have?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1$ &nbsp; **B** $2$ &nbsp; **C** $3$ &nbsp; **D** $4$
:::

$\lvert f\rvert=4$ means $f=4$ or $f=-4$. Because $-4$ is [exactly the minimum]{.hl}, $f=-4$ is reached
at just one point.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — $\lvert f(x)\rvert = k$ where $k$ equals the depth of the dip (a tangent)
:::


$f(x)=(x-3)(x+1)$, minimum $(1,-4)$.

- $f(x)=4:\ x^2-2x-7=0\Rightarrow x=1\pm2\sqrt2$ — **2 solutions**.
- $f(x)=-4:\ x^2-2x+1=0\Rightarrow(x-1)^2=0\Rightarrow x=1$ — **1 solution** (the graph just touches).

Total **3** — **C**.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "y=|x²−2x−3| meets y=4 three times: twice on the flipped arms, once at x=1 where the original touched its minimum −4."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
C='#1f77b4'; L='#d62728'; H='#2ca02c'
x=np.linspace(-3.5,5.5,600); f=x**2-2*x-3
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4,3.6))
ax.plot(x,np.abs(f),color=C,lw=2,label='y=|f(x)|')
ax.axhline(4,color=L,ls='--',lw=1.2,label='y=4')
for xi in (1-2*np.sqrt(2),1+2*np.sqrt(2),1): ax.plot(xi,4,'o',color=H)
ax.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y'); ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.set_ylim(-0.3,8)
ax.set_title('|f(x)| = 4  →  3 solutions (a tangent at x=1)',fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*When $k$ is bigger than the depth you would get four; when $k$ is smaller, four as well but differently
placed; exactly at the depth, the two middle solutions merge into one. Reading that depth is the whole
question.* $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}

:::

## Question 20

::: {.question}
The graph of $y=f(x)$ has range $-1\le f(x)\le4$. Find the difference between the maximum and minimum
values of
$$\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^3 - 3\bigl(f(x)\bigr)^2.$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $16$ &nbsp; **B** $20$ &nbsp; **C** $4$ &nbsp; **D** $27$ &nbsp; **E** $12$
:::

Let $w=f(x)\in[-1,4]$; $g(w)=w^3-3w^2$ now has **two** turning points. Evaluate [both of them and both
endpoints]{.hl} — four candidates.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — cubic in $w$ on an interval with negatives: **two** turning points *and* two endpoints
:::


$g'(w)=3w^2-6w=3w(w-2)=0\Rightarrow w=0$ or $w=2$. The four candidates on $[-1,4]$:
$$g(-1)=-1-3=-4,\quad g(0)=0,\quad g(2)=8-12=-4,\quad g(4)=64-48=16.$$

Maximum $16$ (at $w=4$), minimum $-4$ (at **both** $w=-1$ and $w=2$). Difference $16-(-4)=20$ — **B**.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "g(w)=w³−3w² on [−1,4]. Two turning points (w=0 max-ish, w=2 local min) and two endpoints; overall max 16 at w=4, min −4 (tied at w=−1 and w=2)."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
C='#1f77b4'; MIN='#d62728'; MAX='#2ca02c'
w=np.linspace(-1,4,400); g=w**3-3*w**2
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2,3.8))
ax.plot(w,g,color=C,lw=2)
for pt in [(-1,-4),(2,-4)]:
    ax.plot(*pt,'o',color=MIN)
ax.annotate('−4 (tie)',(2,-4),(2.1,-2.5),color=MIN,fontsize=9)
ax.plot(4,16,'o',color=MAX); ax.annotate('(4, 16) max',(4,16),(1.3,12),color=MAX,fontsize=9)
ax.plot(0,0,'o',color='0.5'); ax.axhline(0,color='0.6',lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('w'); ax.set_ylabel('g(w)'); ax.set_xlim(-1.1,4.1)
ax.set_title(r'$g(w)=w^3-3w^2$ on $[-1,4]$',fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*With a negative in the range, a cubic can have two turning points inside — miss one and you may miss the
minimum. Always list every stationary point **and** both endpoints, then pick the biggest and smallest.*
$\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The two habits to leave with

1. **Transform:** *outside as it says, inside opposite*; $f(ax)$ by $\tfrac1a$; solve "input $=$ old
   input" for a feature's new position; reflection in the $x$-axis swaps max and min.
2. **Function of a function:** write $w=f(x)$, get the range of $w$, then it is an ordinary max/min —
   **turning points *and* endpoints**. For counts, solve for $w$ first, then count preimages.
:::

:::
